why: Visitors need to know what the shop does. A clear heading helps them decide whether to contact it.
lookFor: Read the heading on the page. Compare it with the words in the input.
projectStart: Choose one service and its visitor. Write: ‘This page helps ___ to ___.’ Ask AI to make a page for that task.
explainFocus: Explain who your page helps, which words they see, and what its Contact button actually does.

why: ‘Make it impressive’ leaves a builder guessing. A clear request names one change and a way to check it.
lookFor: Compare the vague request with the example. Find the named section, the change, and the check. The local checker only recognises a few phrases.
projectStart: Look at a page and name one confusing part. Write one change you want AI to make and how you will check the result.
explainFocus: Explain the visitor’s problem, your exact request, and what you observed after the change.

why: A page’s words, appearance and button actions have different jobs. Knowing the difference helps you ask AI for the right change.
lookFor: Watch the heading become bigger. Its words stay the same. Later, try changing the words or the button’s rule separately.
projectStart: Open your service page. Ask AI to show where its words, styles and button actions come from. Draw three labelled boxes.
explainFocus: Point to one piece of content, one style and one action in your actual page. Explain what each controls.

why: A price estimate should not invent an amount when a customer leaves the quantity blank. The app needs a rule before multiplying.
lookFor: An empty quantity stops the estimate. Then enter 0 and 2. Notice that a missing quantity is different from a valid zero.
projectStart: Write what your estimator should do for 2 items, a blank quantity and a negative quantity. Give those examples to AI before it builds.
explainFocus: Explain which inputs your estimator allows, how it calculates an amount, and what happens when the input is invalid.

why: A shop may offer more services tomorrow. One shared rule can turn each service record into a card without copying the whole page.
lookFor: Count the service cards before and after the change. More records should produce more cards using the same pattern.
projectStart: Write three fictional services with an identifier, name and price. Ask AI to display each record using the same card layout.
explainFocus: Explain where your service records live, which rule creates the cards, and how each record is identified.

why: Before building an app, you need to know what problem people actually have. Made-up examples and checked records support different claims.
lookFor: Changing the source changes what the model can claim. A checked count still does not explain why a visit was missed.
projectStart: Choose one real workflow, such as booking a repair. Name where you could learn about it: a person, records, or a clearly labelled practice scenario.
explainFocus: Explain what you observed, where it came from, and which parts are still assumptions.

why: Two missed visits out of ten is different from two out of a hundred. A useful target needs a count and a meaningful total.
lookFor: The missed count stays the same while the total changes. Watch the percentage change. A blank total cannot give a known rate.
projectStart: Write the problem, who it affects, and the result you want to improve. Name the count, total and source you would use to measure it.
explainFocus: Explain what your measure counts, which cases belong in the total, and what evidence would show an improvement.

why: A person confirming a visit needs to know whether it worked. If something fails, keeping their input helps them try again.
lookFor: A visit identifier gives the request something to refer to. Check the displayed outcome; filling an identifier alone does not fix every missing condition.
projectStart: Draw a person’s steps from opening a visit to seeing its result. Include a missing identifier and a lost connection, not just the successful path.
explainFocus: Explain what the person enters, how your app reports the result, and what remains available after a failure.

why: Choosing a tool means comparing what it can do and what it costs over time. A cheap option may still miss a required feature.
lookFor: Changing the number of months changes the cost comparison. Also check whether each option supports the required capability.
projectStart: List what your project must do. Compare two possible approaches over the same time period, including where you can keep or export the data.
explainFocus: Explain why your choice fits the requirements, the time period you compared, and one trade-off you accepted.

why: A success message can appear even when the wrong record changed. You need a check of the result that actually matters.
lookFor: Compare the intended visit with the records before and after the action. Notice whether the check catches the wrong update.
projectStart: Choose three important actions in your project. For each, write the starting state, the action and the exact result you expect to observe.
explainFocus: Explain how your checks distinguish a correct result from a message that merely says it worked.

why: A browser and a server work in different places. If a response is slow, the browser may stop waiting before the server’s outcome is known.
lookFor: Compare response delay with the browser’s waiting limit. A timeout means the wait ended; it does not by itself prove the server cancelled the work.
projectStart: Pick one action, such as confirming a visit. Ask AI to connect a page to a small server and show the request and response between them.
explainFocus: Trace your action from browser to server and back. Explain what your user sees when the response is delayed.

why: Appointments should not vanish when a program restarts. You also need a way to find the right visit when two people share a name.
lookFor: Restarting loses records held only in process memory. Try persistent storage next. Use a visit identifier to tell same-name records apart.
projectStart: Choose the information one appointment needs. Ask AI to save two fictional appointments and show how to find one after restarting the app.
explainFocus: Explain where records are stored, what survives a restart, and which identifier selects one exact appointment.

why: Two people can ask for the last appointment at the same time. Checking and reserving together helps prevent both from claiming it.
lookFor: An atomic rule means ‘check and reserve as one step’. Compare which requests fit and which are refused when there is only one slot.
projectStart: Write the rule ‘accepted bookings must not exceed available slots’. Ask AI to demonstrate two competing requests and a retry of the same request.
explainFocus: Explain how your booking rule protects capacity and how it recognises a repeated attempt at the same booking.

why: Signing in proves who is asking. A separate rule must decide which customer’s visit that person may read.
lookFor: Compare the signed-in customer with the record’s owner. With the trusted check enabled, a different owner should cause a refusal.
projectStart: Write who may read and change each kind of visit. Ask AI to show one allowed request and one refused request using fictional accounts.
explainFocus: Explain how your app identifies the caller, where it checks permission, and what an unauthorised caller receives.

why: Sending a reminder involves another service. Your app needs its configuration and must report only the delivery status it can actually support.
lookFor: Configuration is one requirement, not proof of delivery. Read the resulting status: accepted, unavailable and delivered mean different things.
projectStart: Ask AI to inspect a reminder service’s test mode and required configuration names. Use fictional messages and define how your app will show each outcome.
explainFocus: Explain the boundary between your app and the provider, what status you know, and how you handle a failed or uncertain attempt.

why: An AI agent needs a clear task, limits and permission. Giving it more time or budget cannot grant permission it does not have.
lookFor: Compare the budget with the authority check. Extra budget may allow more work, but a missing permission should still stop the protected action.
projectStart: Choose one small improvement. Write the desired result, files it may change, actions it may take, spending limit and when it must stop.
explainFocus: Explain what you delegated, which boundaries applied, and how you checked the agent’s actual work.

why: Two people or agents can build different parts, but those parts must agree on the information they exchange. More workers cannot fix a naming mismatch.
lookFor: Compare the field name sent by the server with the name read by the interface. Matching those names fixes this model’s connection.
projectStart: Draw which parts depend on which others. Write the shared field names before asking AI to change the page and server.
explainFocus: Explain what each part expects, how you kept those expectations aligned, and how you checked the combined result.

why: An AI answer can look neatly formatted while inventing a fact. A repair-note helper must keep an unknown date unknown.
lookFor: The example replaces the invented date with null, meaning ‘unknown’. Compare the format checks with the separate check against the supplied facts.
projectStart: Choose one useful job for a note assistant. Write what information it may receive, what it should return, and what it must do when information is missing.
explainFocus: Explain why your feature uses AI, which facts support its answer, and how you handle missing or unsupported information.

why: An assistant needs relevant, current information. Reading a document does not give it permission to carry out every instruction inside that document.
lookFor: A current policy can improve the source check. Also inspect relevance and separate action permission; one useful source does not satisfy every boundary.
projectStart: Choose the documents your assistant may use and the actions it may take. Write a safe response for a missing source or missing permission.
explainFocus: Explain where an answer’s supporting information comes from and how action permission is checked separately.

why: An urgent-message helper can raise false alarms or miss important messages. Changing its cutoff trades one kind of mistake against another.
lookFor: Raise the threshold and watch the same labelled cases change category. Compare false alerts with missed urgent cases, not just the alert count.
projectStart: Write example messages with expected outcomes before comparing approaches. Include ordinary, missing-information and misleading cases, and decide which errors cost more.
explainFocus: Explain the cases you tested, the mistakes each approach made, and why your chosen trade-off fits the users.

why: A useful test must be able to expose a real mistake. Checking a friendly message alone can miss an update to the wrong appointment.
lookFor: Read the intended record and the actual changed record. Notice whether the selected check fails when the model has a defect.
projectStart: Choose one important rule in your app. Ask AI for a check that passes when it works and fails when a deliberate mistake is introduced.
explainFocus: Explain what your check observes and show a defect that makes it fail. Keep unrun checks labelled as unrun.

why: A release needs working code and the right settings. Returning to older code does not automatically restore an older data structure.
lookFor: Supplying configuration satisfies one release requirement. Later, compare the running code with the data version after a rollback.
projectStart: Ask AI to inspect how your app starts and is released. List required setting names, a release check and a way to return to a working version.
explainFocus: Explain what your release changes, which checks you ran, and what your recovery plan does to code and stored data.

why: A slow app can spend time in several places. Measuring each step helps you investigate the part that is actually taking the time.
lookFor: Select the provider step and read its duration. Compare all measured steps before deciding what to investigate; the longest step can change.
projectStart: Write one visible symptom and two possible causes. Ask AI to gather observations that could distinguish them before changing the app.
explainFocus: Explain your hypothesis, the evidence you inspected, the change you made, and the new observation used to check recovery.

why: Reusing a saved copy can reduce repeated work. That copy is called a cache, and it may become out of date when the source changes.
lookFor: Follow whether a read uses the source or a cached copy. Check the copy’s age and freshness as well as the amount of work saved.
projectStart: Choose one repeated operation. Measure it with representative examples, try one improvement with AI, and check that the answers are still correct.
explainFocus: Explain what work you reduced, what you measured, and how your app handles old copies or queued requests.

why: A system change can damage information people trust. Restoring a backup is useful only if the right records can actually be recovered and checked.
lookFor: Compare the restored records with the saved snapshot. Restored data and a verified lookup are separate observations.
projectStart: Choose a harmless practice copy of your data. Write what must survive a change and rehearse restoring and checking that copy with AI.
explainFocus: Explain what was backed up, what the change affected, what you restored and how you verified the recovered information.

why: A real project starts by finding what prevents the useful result. Preparing faster cannot get a repair van past a missing site approval.
lookFor: The van stays blocked when preparation becomes faster but approval is still missing. Compare speed with the actual access requirement.
projectStart: Choose a real domain or a clearly labelled practice scenario. Identify a person, their desired result, and the evidence and access you can use.
explainFocus: Explain the outcome you chose, the actual obstacle, what supports that conclusion and what still needs investigation.

why: Your system needs parts that can support the required job. Public page files alone cannot provide shared private customer records.
lookFor: Turning on shared private records adds a requirement. Inspect which parts are now needed and whether the proposed system supplies them.
projectStart: Use your independent project brief. Give AI the user’s task, required behaviour, allowed data and operating limits before it proposes a system.
explainFocus: Explain why each part of your independent solution exists and trace one real action through the parts.

why: An improvement helps only if people use it and the work saved outweighs new work it creates. A faster step can still make the whole process worse.
lookFor: Reduce correction work and compare the net time saved. Also check how many people actually use the change.
projectStart: Choose a small, agreed pilot for your project. Decide who will try it, what result you will measure and what would make you stop or revise it.
explainFocus: Explain what happened in use, how it compared with the earlier process, and which feedback led to your next change.

why: A project must remain usable when another person takes over or a provider changes. Instructions, access and a working connection all matter.
lookFor: Preparing a guide and access does not guarantee that the replacement provider fits. Read the field check and inspect any mismatch.
projectStart: Prepare instructions for opening, configuring and recovering your project. Include the required access and ask someone else to try a full journey.
explainFocus: Explain what the next operator needs, what changed at the provider boundary, and what their actual trial showed.

why: Delivering software means adapting to the user’s actual needs and explaining the result. A new private-data requirement may need a different system.
lookFor: Change the requirement to private customer information. Compare the required parts with those supplied by the selected design.
projectStart: Gather your independent project, its opening instructions, observations and system explanation. If you have not built it yet, begin the project sequence in Lesson 26.
explainFocus: Demonstrate one real user journey, explain your choices and limits, and show how you respond when a reviewer changes a requirement.
